claims.text: The initial material consists of tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten regions embedded in a pure copper matrix.
Conventionally fabricated W–Cu composites, including SPS and vapor-coated-powder products, typically suffer from phase separation and interfacial voids.
Approximately 5 vol% Ni should be added to the copper powder before consolidation.
Powder alloying or mixing followed by SPS is a viable consolidation route for the proposed W–Cu–Ni composite.
SPS below 1200 °C under a reducing or protective atmosphere can produce the proposed composite while avoiding tungsten melting and oxidation.
Adding about 5 vol% Ni will create a transient Ni-rich interlayer or liquid phase at the W–Cu interface during SPS.
The transient Ni-rich phase will wet both tungsten and copper.
Nickel lowers the interfacial energy at the W–Cu interface.
Improved wetting by the Ni-rich phase will fill interfacial microvoids.
The Ni-rich phase will mitigate phase separation and produce a graded, more uniform interface.
After cooling, the graded W–Cu–Ni interface will remain intact.
Compared with Ni-free SPS W–Cu, the Ni-modified composite will have a significantly lower interfacial void fraction.
Compared with Ni-free SPS W–Cu, the Ni-modified composite will have enhanced thermal conductivity.
The Ni-modified composite will maintain mechanical durability under high thermal loads and irradiation-simulated testing.
The benefits will persist in fusion-reactor-joint service provided that the transient Ni phase fully resolves during cooling.

Failure to obtain statistically significant void reduction, improved thermal conductivity, and maintained or improved mechanical performance relative to an identically processed Ni-free control would falsify the hypothesis.
